items.item: The hook's real lesson is that a producer's own green CI was never evidence of safety for anyone except the producer -- 'all tests pass' only ever meant 'nothing I wrote checks for breaks,' and a consumer reading the table was never one of the things being checked.

A reader might assume the CI gate and the runtime check are redundant, two copies of the same safety net -- they protect against different failure modes: the CI gate only ever sees a change that goes through a pull request, while the runtime check is the only thing that can catch a write that bypasses the pipeline's own process entirely.

at.step: Reveal: runtime enforcement catches the out-of-band write

items.item: The breaking-change classifier's real safety property is conservative by construction -- it only calls a removed field 'migrated' when some new field explicitly names what it deprecates, so a rename that merely happens to look similar, without that explicit link, is correctly treated as a silent disappearance rather than a documented migration.

Automated lineage-driven notification doesn't make a breaking change safe to ship -- it only ever runs on a change the CI gate has already approved as non-breaking or as carrying a real migration path; it closes the 'nobody remembered to tell them' gap, not the 'this change breaks them' gap, which the gate already closed earlier.

at.step: Reveal: automated owner notification via lineage

items.item: This topic's contract reuses, rather than reinvents, vocabulary from three earlier topics: the expand/migrate/contract rollout discipline (topic 14), the SLI/SLO/error-budget vocabulary inside the contract's own SLA section (topic 11), and the lineage mechanism driving notification (topic 8's asset model) -- the new thing here is only that a single contract file now makes all three automatically enforceable together.

A reader might assume ODCS's four sections (schema, quality, SLA, team) are independent of each other -- ODCS's own documentation says schema 'is the support for' data quality, meaning the quality rules are only meaningful once the schema they check against is itself declared; the sections are layered, not parallel.

The contract's own quality rules and the breaking-change classifier check two different things that are easy to conflate: quality rules check whether the data currently satisfies promises already made, while breaking-change classification checks whether a proposed schema change would silently revoke a promise an existing consumer is relying on.

GoCardless's own account of the problem (the hook's real-world basis) predates ODCS specifically as a standard -- the pattern this topic demonstrates (contract-as-code, enforced in CI, with lineage-driven notification) is a later, more structured answer to exactly the informal pain GoCardless first wrote about.

This topic deliberately leaves out building a real catalog-backed lineage system -- the lineage graph driving notification is topic 8's and Chapter 13's mechanism, used here as a small synthetic stand-in rather than independently built or re-taught.

The contract's SLA section and topic 11's error-budget vocabulary describe the same kind of commitment at two different layers -- an SLO is a target a platform team sets and tracks operationally, while an SLA entry in the contract is that same target written down as a promise to a specific named consumer, which is what makes it something CI or runtime enforcement can actually check.
